reading.title: The girl who played it safe

A2.text:
Nigar is an accountant. She is very careful. She always plays it safe. She never drives over the speed limit, and she does not like surprises.

Her friends are different. They love thrills and adrenaline. In May, they went to the mountains in Gabala. There was a long zipline over a deep valley.

“Come on, Nigar!” her friend Aysel said. “I dare you to try it.”

Nigar looked down. The valley was very deep. She was terrified. “No,” she said. “That is reckless.”

The instructor smiled. “It is safe. You have a helmet and strong ropes,” he said.

Nigar watched her friends. They screamed and laughed. Nigar thought, “I always play it safe. Maybe I can live on the edge, just for one minute.”

She decided to take the plunge. She put on the helmet. Her legs were shaking. Then she jumped.

The wind was in her face. The valley was green and beautiful. She felt a big rush of happiness. She screamed, but it was a happy scream.

At the bottom, her friends clapped. “How was it?” Aysel asked.

Nigar's face was red, and her eyes were bright. “Again!” she said. “I want to do it again!”

Her friends laughed. The careful accountant had a new hobby.

B1.text:
Nigar was famous among her friends for one thing: she always played it safe. She was an accountant who checked every receipt twice, drove ten kilometres below the speed limit and booked holidays a year in advance. Her friends, on the other hand, collected thrills the way other people collect stamps.

In May, they persuaded her to join them on a weekend in Gabala. On Saturday morning, they took the cable car up the mountain to the start of a zipline — a thin steel cable stretching nearly a kilometre across a green valley.

“Come on, Nigar,” said her friend Aysel, already wearing her helmet. “I dare you.”

Nigar walked to the edge and looked down. The trees below looked like broccoli. She was absolutely terrified. “This isn't brave,” she said. “It's reckless.”

The instructor, a calm young man from Gabala, showed her the double harness and the helmet. “Three thousand people did this last year,” he said. “Not one accident. The only risk is that you'll like it.”

One by one, her friends flew off the platform, screaming with joy. Nigar stood alone, her heart pounding. All her life she had watched other people live on the edge. She had never once found out what it felt like.

“Just once,” she told herself. “Take the plunge.”

She clipped in, closed her eyes and stepped off.

For the first second, there was nothing but fear. Then she opened her eyes. The valley opened beneath her like a map, the wind rushed past her ears, and something she had never felt before filled her chest — pure adrenaline. She heard someone screaming with laughter and realised it was her.

At the bottom, her friends were waiting. Aysel took one look at her red cheeks and wild hair and started laughing. “Well? Never again?”

Nigar was already unclipping her harness. “How long,” she asked breathlessly, “is the queue to go back up?”

B2.text:
Among her friends, Nigar was renowned for a single quality: she always played it safe. An accountant by profession and by temperament, she checked every receipt twice, drove a disciplined ten kilometres under the speed limit and booked her holidays eleven months ahead. Her friends, by contrast, collected thrills the way other people collect fridge magnets.

That May, after weeks of persuasion, they lured her to Gabala for the weekend. On Saturday morning they rode the cable car up the mountain to the launch platform of a zipline — a slender steel cable strung almost a kilometre across a plunging green valley.

“Come on, Nigar,” said her friend Aysel, already fastening her helmet. “I dare you.”

Nigar approached the edge and peered over. The forest below resembled a tray of broccoli. She was, in the most literal sense, terrified. “This isn't courage,” she said. “It's simply reckless.”

The instructor, an unhurried young man from a nearby village, demonstrated the double harness and tapped her helmet. “Three thousand people last season,” he said. “Not a single accident. The only real danger is that you'll enjoy it.”

One after another, her friends launched themselves off the platform, whooping as they vanished into the valley. Nigar remained, heart hammering against her ribs. All her life she had watched other people live on the edge, observing from a sensible distance. She had never once discovered what it actually felt like.

“Once,” she said under her breath. “Just once. Take the plunge.”

She clipped in, shut her eyes and stepped into nothing.

For one endless second there was only fear. Then she opened her eyes, and the valley unfurled beneath her like a living map, the wind roaring past her ears, and a sensation she had never known flooded her chest — a pure, electric rush of adrenaline. Somewhere, someone was shrieking with laughter. It took her a moment to realise it was her.

Her friends were waiting at the landing platform. Aysel took one look at her flushed cheeks and wind-wrecked hair and dissolved into giggles. “Well? Never again?”

Nigar was already wrestling with her harness buckle. “How long,” she gasped, “is the queue to go back up?”

podcast.title: I dare you

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Do you like speed and adrenaline? Guess: what did Sam do in the mountains last weekend?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is speed and thrills. Leyla, are you an adrenaline person?
Not at all. I play it safe. Even a fast lift makes me nervous.
[laugh] Then you'll love my story. Last weekend in Gabala, I did a zipline in the mountains.
Over the valley? How high is it?
High enough. When I stood at the start, I was terrified. My legs were shaking.
So why did you do it?
My friends from running club. One of them said, "I dare you." And I can never say no to a dare.
And how was it?
The first second was horrible. Then — pure thrill. I was screaming and laughing at the same time.
That's the adrenaline. My cousin Rashad loves that feeling. He rides a motorbike.
Fast?
Too fast. My aunt is always worried. At least he always wears a helmet.
And the speed limit?
[chuckle] He says he knows it. I'm not sure he follows it.
When I run, I feel a small rush too, especially at the end of a race. That's my kind of speed.
That I understand. Okay, I have a confession. Last summer I went on the big wheel on the boulevard.
The big wheel is slow, Leyla.
For me it was a big step! Next year maybe I'll take the plunge and try the zipline.
I'll hold your bag. And film everything. [laugh]
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what is the most exciting thing you have ever done — and would you do it again?
Mine is the zipline. And yes — tomorrow. See you next time!
Bye for now!
